_comment: The act roster as data. Built 2026-08-15 from the restructure spec and signet-roster-system-v2.xlsx. Nothing about an act is hardcoded in a page: act pages, roster cards, filter UI, per-act Offer schema and llms.txt all render from this file. The schema is deliberately flat and tag-based so it exports cleanly to the intranet/CRM later.
_source_note: The spec names signet-roster-final.xlsx as the content source. That file does not exist in the repo. The only roster workbook present is signet-roster-system-v2.xlsx, and this file is populated from its Roster and Chair Specs tabs. If a 'final' workbook exists elsewhere, diff it against this before launch.
_pricing_note: Per-config prices are NOT stored on acts. Each ladder rung names a rateCard config id and the build reads the range from rateCard below, so an act page and the pricing page can never disagree. The provisional per-act floors in the workbook (Dirty Flamenco 1800/2500, Tejas 1000/1400, and so on) are deliberately NOT used: the workbook's own legend calls them provisional, and they sit well under the spec rate card. The spec rate card is the authority.
_spelling_note: Tejas Singh, with the h. The restructure spec and the roster workbook both wrote 'Tejas Sing'; Daniel confirmed 2026-08-16 that the workbook was wrong, and it has been corrected at source (signet-roster-system-v2.xlsx, Roster!B11/E11 and Chair Specs!A11/B11). The act slug changed with it, /music/tejas-sing/ to /music/tejas-singh/, while the page was under an hour old. Do not 'fix' this back to match an older copy of the spec.
_players_note: No player names, no lineup, no 'collective of musicians' framing. The face is the one name published for an act, because the face is what the client buys. Instrumentation is published where it is part of the product (upright bass and guitar for a jazz duo); the people holding those chairs are not.

acts.name: Dirty Flamenco
acts.alt: A trumpet resting on a table.
acts.blurb: The only flamenco act on this roster, and close to the only one in Colorado sold as a private event product rather than a concert booking. Real palos, played by a group with a standing book. Book it when the room needs one thing guests photograph.
acts.seo_title: Dirty Flamenco: flamenco trio for private events in Denver
acts.meta_description: Flamenco for weddings, corporate dinners and private events in Denver and the Colorado mountains. Trio from $2,800, with dancer and percussion configurations. Rates published.
identity: Flamenco is the one booking on this roster that nobody else in Colorado sells as a private event product. It exists here as a concert act, or as a guitarist playing Spanish-flavored background. Dirty Flamenco is neither. It is a working group with a standing book, sold at private event scale.

That matters for a specific kind of night. Most live music at a private event is designed to be felt and not watched. This is the opposite booking. It is the act you hire when the program has a moment in it that needs to be the moment: a cultural centerpiece, a corporate dinner that has to be memorable rather than pleasant, a reception that wants something guests will describe to people who were not there.

The book is palos, the traditional forms, not a set of pop songs with nylon strings on them. That is the difference between a flamenco booking and a Spanish guitar booking, and it is audible inside eight bars.

ladder.bestFor: Cocktails and dinner. Full volume range without a dance floor.
A program with a set-piece in it. The dancer is what the room turns to watch.

ladder.build: The trio plus dancer and second percussion
ladder.bestFor: Large rooms and outdoor events, where a cajon alone will not carry.

setlist.note: Flamenco is organized by palo, the traditional form, rather than by song title. A set is built from these and shaped to the room on the night. Representative, not fixed.

acts.name: Jordan Lovinger & DF
acts.alt: A trumpet resting on a table.
acts.blurb: Standards on upright bass and guitar, played at the volume of the room. The booking for arrival, cocktails and dinner, when the music has to hold the room without anybody having to raise their voice over it.
acts.seo_title: Jordan Lovinger & DF: jazz duo for cocktails and dinner in Denver
acts.meta_description: Jazz standards duo for private events in Denver and the Colorado mountains. Upright bass and guitar for cocktails and dinner. $1,050 for an hour, $2,000 for the cocktail and dinner block.
identity: This is the cocktail hour booking. Upright bass and guitar, playing the standards book, at a volume you can talk across.

Most of what goes wrong in the first two hours of an event is a volume decision, not a repertoire decision. A band that plays this hour at the level it plays the dance floor makes guests shout at each other while they are still deciding what kind of night it is. A duo is the honest instrument for it: two players cannot get loud by accident, and the arrangement stays open enough that conversation sits on top of it rather than under it.

Standards are the book because they are the one repertoire nobody has to be told about. Guests do not identify the tunes and do not need to. The room reads as expensive and unhurried, which is the whole job for that hour.
The duo covers arrival, cocktails and dinner on one line of the contract. If the night also needs a dance floor, that is a second act rather than this one turning up.

ladder.bestFor: Arrival, cocktails and dinner. One hour or the whole front of the night.

setlist.note: The standards book. A set is pulled from it and paced to the room rather than played in order. Representative, not fixed.

acts.name: Tejas Singh
acts.alt: A snare drum with sticks laid across it and a close microphone.
acts.blurb: The only act here that ladders. A duo at six o'clock and a quartet at ten, same face, same book, one contract. At quartet and up this is the biggest thing on the roster and the one to book when the floor has to fill.
acts.seo_title: Tejas Singh: cover band for weddings and private events in Denver
acts.meta_description: Voice-fronted covers for private events in Denver and the Colorado mountains. Duo for cocktails from $2,000, quartet for the dance floor from $4,000. Every rate published.
identity: One act, four sizes. This is the only booking on the roster that changes shape during the night instead of being replaced.

The reason to care is the contract. Most events buy the front of the night and the back of the night from two different acts, which means two load-ins, two sound checks, two sets of names to keep straight and a seam in the middle that guests can hear. This ladders instead: a duo through arrival and dinner, then the rhythm section arrives and the same voice fronts the dance floor. The room experiences one band getting bigger.

At quartet and above it stops being a cocktail act. Voice, guitar, bass and drums playing a covers book built for a floor is the largest live format on this roster, and it is the one to book when filling the floor is the actual objective rather than a hope.
It is a premium cover band. It is not a show band. Nobody changes costume, there is no choreography and there is no host segment. The band plays, reads the floor, and plays the next thing.

ladder.bestFor: Small rooms, and parties that want a floor without a full band.

ladder.build: The trio plus keys or a second guitar
ladder.bestFor: The dance floor booking. Weddings and corporate parties.

ladder.build: The quartet plus a horn or a second voice
ladder.bestFor: Large rooms, galas, and anything that has to sound like an event rather than a band.

setlist.note: Pulled from the full song book, which runs past 240 titles and is published in its own right. A set is built against your run of show and read song by song on the night. Representative, not fixed.

acts.name: Dan Steele
acts.alt: A snare drum with sticks laid across it and a close microphone.
acts.blurb: Voice-fronted funk and soul for a small room. The singer is the front of this band, so the set leans on the vocal end of the funk book: Motown, Stax, the songs a room sings back. Book it where the dance floor is close to the tables.
acts._face_chair_note: The workbook marks this act's face chair as assumed (vox/keys) and flags the overlap with DF Funk. The voice-fronted framing here is what differentiates the two listings and it rests on that assumed chair. Confirm with Dan Steele before launch; if the chair is wrong, this blurb is wrong.

acts.name: DF Funk
acts.alt: A snare drum with sticks laid across it and a close microphone.
acts.blurb: Guitar-fronted funk, built on the groove rather than the vocal. Instrumental heads, longer pockets, and a set that works as hard at background volume as it does on a floor. The one to book when the room wants funk without a frontman working it.

acts.name: Thomas Owen Band
acts.alt: An empty room set for an event before doors.
acts.blurb: Americana for a patio and the daylight end of an event. Roots, country and folk-rock played by a trio that can sit at conversation volume for three hours without going flat. Outdoor ceremonies, welcome parties and long afternoons.
acts._promote_note: Spec: promote to flagship when footage exists. The workbook also flags this act as originals-first with an open question about whether it can field a two hour covers set. The material field says covers and originals on that basis. Resolve the covers question before promoting.

acts.name: Josh
acts.alt: Faders and knobs on a mixing console.
acts.blurb: Open format DJ, on its own or carrying the late end after a band steps off. Adding a live instrument over the decks, bass or saxophone, is a named option rather than a favor: it is the format roughly one couple in six now asks for, and it is priced on the rate card.

hybrid.label: DJ plus live instrument
hybrid.copy: A player on the floor over the DJ set. It is the difference between a playlist and a room watching something happen, and it holds a dance floor through the hours a band would have gone home.

acts._name_note: The act is listed with a first name only, per the workbook and the spec. A single first name reads thin next to eight other named acts on the roster page. Worth a surname or a DJ name before launch.

acts.name: Tony Medina
acts.alt: An empty room set for an event before doors.
acts.blurb: Blues-based covers, solo or as a duo, at the smallest spend on this roster. Background music that is actually played rather than streamed. Rehearsal dinners, welcome drinks, office parties and any room where live music is the right idea and a band is the wrong size.
